# Penalized Regression

In Milestone 17 we used cross-validation to tune the probability cutoff for a model that predicts whether a team wins the NCAA national championship using only AdjEM. In this milestone we add more predictors and fit three penalized regression models (ridge, LASSO, and elastic net). We then compare them against our existing model runs.

Penalized regression shrinks the coefficient estimates toward zero. This helps when we have several predictors, especially correlated ones, because it reduces overfitting and helps the model generalize to new seasons.

We use five-fold cross-validation to tune the regularization strength and maximize classification accuracy using our previous cutoff. We then compare the ridge model against our Milestone 17 model to see whether regularization improves our predictions.

## Choose predictors

```{python}


# Predictors selected from our exploratory analysis
predictors = [
    "adj_em",
    "wab_z",
    "sos_rank"
]


```

## Load data. This is the same data prep as Milestone 17. We keep all Division I teams, drop rows missing the key inputs, scale AdjEM, and keep the 2022 and later seasons separate for testing.

```{python}

from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

# Load the validated v2 dataset
data_path = Path("data/processed/champion_checklist_v2.csv")

if not data_path.exists():
    data_path = Path("../data/processed/champion_checklist_v2.csv")

data = pd.read_csv(data_path)

# Keep D1 teams eligible to win the national championship
teams = data.loc[
    ~data["is_reclassifying"].fillna(False)
].copy()

# A non-tournament team is a historical non-champion
teams["champion_label"] = (
    teams["champion"].eq(True)
).astype(int)


# Scale AdjEM to match our previous baseline model
teams["adj_em_5"] = (teams["adj_em"] - 20) / 5


# Keep post-2021 seasons separate for testing
train = teams[teams["season"] <= 2021].copy()
test = teams[teams["season"] >= 2022].copy()

print("Training teams:", len(train))
print("Training champions:", train["champion_label"].sum())
print("Testing teams:", len(test))
print("Testing champions:", test["champion_label"].sum())

```



## Set up the training and test data

Penalized models can't handle missing values, so we drop any team that is missing one of our predictors. We then split each dataset into the predictors (`X`) and the outcome (`y`).

We also set up the same 5-fold cross-validation as Milestone 17. `GroupKFold` keeps all the teams from a season in the same fold, so the model is always validated on seasons it has not seen. Finally, we define the same list of cutoffs and a small helper function that picks the best cutoff by F1 score, the same rule we used in Milestone 17. F1 makes more sense than accuracy here because there is only one champion per season, so a model that flags nobody would still be about 99.7% accurate.

```{python}
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

train_p = train.dropna(subset=predictors)
test_p = test.dropna(subset=predictors)


X_train = train_p[predictors]
y_train = train_p["champion_label"]

X_test = test_p[predictors]
y_test = test_p["champion_label"]

groups = train_p["season"]


print(f"Training teams with complete predictors: {len(train_p)}")
print(f"Test teams with complete predictors: {len(test_p)}")

# 5-fold cross-validation grouped by season
cv = GroupKFold(n_splits=5)

# Same cutoffs as Milestone 17
cutoffs = [0.001, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02,
           0.03, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20]

# Find the cutoff with the best F1 score
def best_cutoff(y, probs):
    rows = []
    for c in cutoffs:
        preds = (np.asarray(probs) >= c).astype(int)
        rows.append({
            "Cutoff": c,
            "Precision": precision_score(y, preds, zero_division=0),
            "Recall": recall_score(y, preds, zero_division=0),
            "F1": f1_score(y, preds, zero_division=0),
        })
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    return df.sort_values(
        ["F1", "Recall", "Cutoff"], ascending=[False, False, True]
    ).iloc[0]
```

## Existing model run: Milestone 17 (AdjEM only)

We rerun the Milestone 17 cross-validation so we have its predicted probabilities to compare against. It is the same logistic regression using only `adj_em_5`, fit with a season-grouped 5-fold split. We use the same teams as the penalized models so the comparison is fair.

```{python}
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

m17_cv_probs = pd.Series(np.nan, index=train_p.index)

for fold, (train_idx, valid_idx) in enumerate(
    cv.split(train_p, groups=train_p["season"]), start=1
):
    fold_train = train_p.iloc[train_idx]
    fold_valid = train_p.iloc[valid_idx]

    model = smf.glm(
        "champion_label ~ adj_em_5",
        data=fold_train,
        family=sm.families.Binomial()
    ).fit()

    m17_cv_probs.loc[fold_valid.index] = model.predict(fold_valid)

assert m17_cv_probs.notna().all()
print("Milestone 17 cross-validation complete!")
```

```{python}

# Use the cutoff selected from our updated Milestone 17 model
m17_cutoff_results = best_cutoff(y_train, m17_cv_probs)
m17_cutoff = float(m17_cutoff_results["Cutoff"])

print(f"Milestone 17 cutoff: {m17_cutoff:.3f}")
print(f"Cross-validation F1: {m17_cutoff_results['F1']:.4f}")

```

## Tune ridge

Use ridge (L2) logistic regression to reduce overfitting by shrinking coefficient estimates toward zero. We standardize the predictors because they have different scales. We use five-fold cross-validation grouped by season to select the regularization strength that maximizes classification accuracy, using the cutoff selected from our Milestone 17 baseline.

```{python}

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# Standardize predictors and fit ridge (L2) logistic regression
ridge_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("feature_engineering", StandardScaler()),
    ("classification", LogisticRegression(
        max_iter=3000,
        solver="lbfgs"
    ))
])

# Try different regularization strengths
C_grid = np.logspace(-3, 3, 13)

# Calculate accuracy using the Milestone 17 cutoff
def cutoff_accuracy(estimator, X, y):
    probabilities = estimator.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
    predictions = (probabilities >= m17_cutoff).astype(int)
    return accuracy_score(y, predictions)

# Tune C using season-grouped 5-fold cross-validation
ridge_tune = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=ridge_pipe,
    param_grid={"classification__C": C_grid},
    scoring=cutoff_accuracy,
    cv=cv,
    refit=True
)

ridge_tune.fit(X_train, y_train, groups=groups)

print("Best C:", ridge_tune.best_params_["classification__C"])
print(f"Best CV accuracy: {ridge_tune.best_score_:.4%}")

```

## Cross-validation comparison

```{python}

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score, precision_score,
    recall_score, f1_score, log_loss
)

# Out-of-fold probabilities for the tuned ridge model
ridge_cv_probs = cross_val_predict(
    ridge_tune.best_estimator_,
    X_train,
    y_train,
    cv=cv,
    groups=groups,
    method="predict_proba"
)[:, 1]

# Compare both models using the SAME cutoff
def evaluate_model(name, probabilities):
    predictions = (
        np.asarray(probabilities) >= m17_cutoff
    ).astype(int)

    return {
        "Model": name,
        "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_train, predictions),
        "Precision": precision_score(
            y_train, predictions, zero_division=0
        ),
        "Recall": recall_score(
            y_train, predictions, zero_division=0
        ),
        "F1": f1_score(
            y_train, predictions, zero_division=0
        ),
        "Log Loss": log_loss(y_train, probabilities),
        "Teams Flagged": int(predictions.sum()),
        "Champions Found": int(
            ((predictions == 1) &
             (y_train.to_numpy() == 1)).sum()
        )
    }

m18_comparison = pd.DataFrame([
    evaluate_model(
        "Milestone 17 (AdjEM)", m17_cv_probs
    ),
    evaluate_model(
        "Milestone 18 (Ridge)", ridge_cv_probs
    )
])

print(m18_comparison.round(5).to_string(index=False))

```

Our ridge model choose a strength of C = 0.001, which was the strongest regularization tested. It got 99.71% accuracy, compared to 99.48% for our previous model

But, even though ridge had higher accuracy, it failed to identify any of the 16 historical champions. At our selected 15% cutoff, it classified every team as a non-champion. The previous model identified 7 of the 16 champions and had a higher F1 score of 0.3333.

Ridge also had a higher log loss (0.01962 compared to 0.01054), meaning its probability predictions performed worse on that metric.

This shows an important limitation of accuracy for our project. Since there is only one national champion each season, a model can achieve extremely high accuracy simply by predicting that no team wins the championship.

## Evaluate on test seasons

```{python}

# Refit the Milestone 17 baseline on all training data
m17_full = smf.glm(
    "champion_label ~ adj_em_5",
    data=train_p,
    family=sm.families.Binomial()
).fit()

# Predict championship probabilities on test seasons
baseline_test_probs = m17_full.predict(test_p)

ridge_test_probs = ridge_tune.best_estimator_.predict_proba(
    X_test
)[:, 1]

# Evaluate both models using the same cutoff
def test_metrics(name, probabilities):
    preds = (
        np.asarray(probabilities) >= m17_cutoff
    ).astype(int)

    actual = y_test.to_numpy()

    return {
        "Model": name,
        "Accuracy": accuracy_score(actual, preds),
        "Precision": precision_score(
            actual, preds, zero_division=0
        ),
        "Recall": recall_score(
            actual, preds, zero_division=0
        ),
        "F1": f1_score(
            actual, preds, zero_division=0
        ),
        "Log Loss": log_loss(actual, probabilities),
        "Teams Flagged": int(preds.sum()),
        "Champions Found": int(
            ((preds == 1) & (actual == 1)).sum()
        )
    }

test_results = pd.DataFrame([
    test_metrics("Milestone 17", baseline_test_probs),
    test_metrics("Milestone 18 Ridge", ridge_test_probs)
])

print(test_results.round(5).to_string(index=False))

```

## Results

We evaluated both models on the 2022–2026 seasons, which were excluded from training and regularization tuning.

The ridge model got 99.72% accuracy, compared to 99.27% for the Milestone 17 model. However, ridge again predicted zero champions, while the previous model correctly identified 3 of the 5 champions.

The previous model also had a lower test log loss of 0.01046, compared to 0.01880 for ridge. This suggests that our earlier model performed better at identifying champions and estimating championship probabilities, despite having slightly lower accuracy.

## Conclusion

Ridge regression successfully improved overall classification accuracy, which was the objective here. But that improvement came at the expense of getting the actual champions.

For this project we care most about getting championship contenders and producing useful probabilities than simply maximizing accuracy. Based on these results, we would favor our Milestone 17 model over this particular ridge model.

In future modeling, we can explore other regularization methods and evaluation metrics that better reflect our championship prediction objective.
